html:
The Sino-Indian War was a one-month border war in the Himalayas in 1962. China won it completely, and the defeat marked India for a generation.

The two countries disputed the border in two places. In the west was Aksai Chin, a high desert that India counted as part of Ladakh; China had quietly built a road across it in the 1950s to link Tibet and Xinjiang. In the east China rejected the McMahon Line, drawn by the British in 1914. Trust collapsed after 1959, when the Dalai Lama fled to India (see the Tibetan exile). India began placing small posts forward in the disputed zones.

On 20 October 1962 Chinese forces attacked on both fronts. Indian troops, few in number, in cotton uniforms and with old rifles at 4,000 metres, were overrun. A second push in November took the passes of the eastern front, and the road to the plains of Assam lay open. Nehru asked the United States for aircraft.

On 21 November China announced a ceasefire and pulled back in the east. It kept Aksai Chin. India lost about 1,400 dead and 4,000 prisoners.

Nehru's policy of friendship with China was finished; he died in 1964. India doubled its defence spending. The border is still not agreed, and soldiers died in a clash there in 2020.
sum: The Sino-Indian War was a one-month border war in the Himalayas in 1962. China won it completely, and the defeat marked India for a generation.
